analysis.one_liner: Permanently restores the estate tax but cuts the rate to 15% and exempts the first $5 million of every estate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2001, Congress passed a law that gradually shrank the estate tax — the tax on very large inheritances — with full repeal scheduled for 2010. This bill, from a conservative-leaning Democrat, would have cancelled that repeal and kept an estate tax permanently, but on much softer terms than existed before 2001: only estates above $5 million would owe anything, and they would pay a flat 15% instead of the roughly 46% top rate in effect in 2006. It also cut the gift tax to 15% and removed a complex accounting rule for inherited assets. The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth more than $5 million would gain the most: their tax rate would drop to a flat 15% (or the capital gains rate if lower), down from a top rate of roughly 46% in 2006, and estates between roughly $2 million and $5 million — which owed tax in 2006 — would owe nothing. Owners of family farms and closely held businesses, the sponsor's stated concern, would be nearly all exempted. Heirs of all inherited assets would benefit from repealing the carryover basis rule, which would otherwise require calculating gains from the deceased's original purchase price.

how_it_helps.text: It sets a permanent $5 million exemption per estate, meaning the vast majority of estates — including nearly all family farms and small businesses — would pay no estate tax at all.

It cuts the tax rate on everything above the exemption to a flat 15% (or the capital gains rate, if lower), far below the roughly 46% top rate in effect in 2006, so even taxable estates would owe far less.

It repeals the 2001 law's carryover basis rule, which would have forced heirs to use the deceased's original purchase price when calculating capital gains — a paperwork and tax burden heirs of even modest inherited property would have faced.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and ultimately other taxpayers — would bear the cost of the lost revenue, since taxing fortunes above $5 million at 15% instead of the pre-2001 graduated rates (up to roughly 46-55%) would sharply reduce what the wealthiest estates contribute. Estates below $5 million pay nothing either way, so ordinary families would see no direct change.
analysis.who_pays_short: Other taxpayers, via lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill would sharply cut taxes on the largest estates: it drops the rate from the pre-2001 schedule (which reached about 46-55%) to 15% and raises the exemption from roughly $2 million to $5 million, so nearly all of the benefit goes to heirs of multi-million-dollar estates.

Cutting the rate to 15% and exempting the first $5 million would cost the federal Treasury substantial revenue relative to the pre-2001 estate tax, leaving other taxpayers or federal programs to absorb the difference.

Supporters of keeping a stronger estate tax would argue that even a 15% rate on fortunes above $5 million lets the largest, untaxed-in-life wealth pass to heirs far more cheaply than the graduated rates that applied before 2001.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's honest upside is certainty and simplicity: it would end the scheduled disappearance and return of the estate tax and lower the rate enough to ease pressure on heirs of family farms and closely held businesses, which was the sponsor's stated concern. The cost is that the relief is badly targeted — the $5 million exemption and 15% rate mean nearly all of the tax cut goes to the largest estates, while the Treasury gives up substantial revenue that other taxpayers would eventually have to make up. Compared with simply letting pre-2001 law stand, the bill was a large transfer to wealthy heirs with little for anyone else. It also carried no offsetting revenue provisions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 18, 2006 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which is where any tax bill must start.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
With only two cosponsors, the bill never built the support needed to move in a committee controlled by the opposing party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly; the bill's death preserved the existing estate tax schedule, which taxed large estates at far higher rates than this bill would have.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal Treasury and the existing estate tax

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and drew one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, but it never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Heirs to very large estates (over $5 million)
industries.note: The bill would tax only estates above $5 million and then at just 15%, so heirs to multi-million-dollar fortunes would owe a fraction of what the pre-2001 law required. Very few families are affected; the benefit is concentrated entirely among them.

industries.industry: Owners of family farms and closely held businesses
industries.note: These owners were the sponsor's stated concern: land- and equipment-rich but cash-poor operations can face estate tax bills their heirs struggle to pay. The $5 million exemption would shield almost all of them, though most already fell under the 2006 exemption.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisors
industries.note: A permanent, simpler estate tax with a flat 15% rate and a single $5 million exemption would reduce the complexity that makes multi-year estate planning lucrative for the very wealthy — while a permanent tax at all keeps some planning demand alive.
